 Latest
 Pinned Tim Balk 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Scott Colom, the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi, held a slim but growing lead on Friday, as election officials continued to count votes in a race that could expand the Senate majority that Democrats secured in the midterm elections.
 The latest vote report showed Mr. Colom leading the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 2,574 votes, according to The Associated Press. If he wins, Mr. Colom would be the first Democrat to capture a Senate seat in Mississippi in 44 years and the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. 
 Democrats wrested back control of the Senate and the House in the midterms on Tuesday, as voters voiced displeasure with rising prices during President Trump’s tumultuous second term. As of Friday evening, Democrats had won at least 253 seats in the House and at least 54 in the Senate , the party’s largest majorities since the first years of the Obama administration.
 But the election officials were still tallying ballots, and those numbers were expected to grow.
 In addition to two Senate races, in Alaska and Mississippi, nearly two dozen House races were still too close to call.
 In Mississippi, lawyers for Ms. Hyde-Smith formally asked election officials on Thursday to preserve provisional ballots, a signal she might challenge the results in court. Mr. Colom’s campaign objected in a letter to election officials to parts of Ms. Hyde-Smith’s request. Mail-in ballots can continue to arrive, and provisional ballots can continue to be verified, until Tuesday. Counties have until Nov. 13 to certify their election results to the state.
 In the Senate race in Alaska, the Democratic challenger, former Representative Mary Peltola, still had a slim lead on Friday over the Republican incumbent. A New York Times analysis indicated that Ms. Peltola’s lead would most likely hold, but it could be days before remaining mail ballots are counted.
 The next batches of votes from Alaska are expected to be posted on Monday and Tuesday, according to the state’s Division of Elections. The race may also require a ranked-choice tabulation, which would not occur until Nov. 18.
 Across the country, Republicans were reckoning with their worst performance since the aftermath of the Watergate scandal a half-century ago. President Trump defended his role in the defeat on social media late Thursday, arguing his party had faced a drubbing because he was not on the ballot.
 But others in the party placed the blame squarely on the president. Senator John Curtis, a Utah Republican, said people had voted against Republicans because of the state of the economy under Mr. Trump’s leadership. “This was about the president and the president’s policies,” he said.
 Here’s what else we’re covering:
 Democratic socialist mayors: Nithya Raman’s victory in the race for Los Angeles mayor makes her the latest democratic socialist to be elected to lead a major U.S. city over the past year. The group includes the mayors of New York, Los Angeles and Seattle. Read more › 
 Transgender athletes: Voters in four states chose to bar transgender athletes from competing on female sports teams. Opinion polls show that most Americans say transgender girls and women should not play on girls’ and women’s sports teams, and the Democratic Party has wrestled with internal divisions on the issue. Read more › 
 Progressive power player: Representative Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 House Democrat, is set to become the majority leader in January. Ms. Clark would make history as the first woman to hold that title, though Representative Nancy Pelosi of California served as House speaker, a loftier role. Read more ›

 Kansans elect a Democrat as attorney general, voting out Kris Kobach. 
 Image Chris Mann, a Democrat, has worked as a police officer and prosecutor. Credit... Charlie Riedel/Associated Press Kris W. Kobach, Kansas’ Republican attorney general, helped to make claims of widespread illegal voting a potent political issue years before President Trump became the party’s leader.
 But Mr. Kobach was denied another term by voters, The Associated Press reported on Friday. The result demonstrated both how Kansas and Mr. Kobach’s own trajectory have shifted since he crashed onto the national political landscape more than 20 years ago.
 Chris Mann, a Democrat who has worked as a police officer and prosecutor, defeated Mr. Kobach, marking the first time in 20 years that Kansans have elected a Democrat as attorney general.
 It was a momentous election for Democrats in Kansas and across the country. Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor and centrist Democrat, became the first member of his party to win a Senate race in Kansas since the 1930s. He unseated Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican and close ally of President Trump. And in the governor’s race, Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee, was leading in a close contest that had not yet been called.
 Mr. Kobach was, in many ways, ahead of his political time. As a law professor and Justice Department official in the 2000s, he pushed for tighter immigration laws . And as Kansas’ secretary of state in the 2010s, he sought and received the authority to prosecute people for illegally voting, making national headlines with the handful of cases he pursued .
 Image Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican, helped to make claims of widespread illegal voting a potent political issue years before President Trump became the party’s leader. Credit... Charlie Riedel/Associated Press Though studies have shown that a very small percentage of ballots are cast by noncitizens, Mr. Kobach’s focus on the issue helped to elevate illegal voting as a national issue years before Mr. Trump seized on it during his presidential campaigns. During his first term as president, Mr. Trump tapped Mr. Kobach to lead a panel on voter fraud.
 While Mr. Kobach’s message resonated, his own record was more mixed. A federal judge once found him in contempt of court . And Mr. Kobach lost his campaign for governor in 2018 to Laura Kelly, a Democrat, before losing the Republican primary for Senate in 2020. He returned to statewide office four years ago after narrowly defeating Mr. Mann to win a first term as attorney general .
 As attorney general, Mr. Kobach has defended a state law restricting gender-transition treatments for minors and pushed unsuccessfully for an elected State Supreme Court . His office also prosecuted the Mexican-born mayor of a small Kansas town, who admitted to voting in U.S. elections without being a citizen, in a case that captured the attention of the Trump administration.
 Though Mr. Kobach was once seen as an outlier among Republicans, his views on immigration and voting have become centerpieces of the party’s platform during the Trump era. But in that same period, Republicans’ hold on Kansas has slipped somewhat.
 Republicans continue to win presidential elections in Kansas by large margins, but Ms. Kelly won two terms as governor and the once-conservative suburbs of Kansas City have turned blue, repeatedly electing Representative Sharice Davids, a Democrat, to Congress.

Nate Cohn, The New York Times’s chief political analyst, explains. Advertisement

 Nancy Lacore, a Democratic former Navy admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, flipped the South Carolina House seat held by Representative Nancy Mace, a Republican who ran unsuccessfully for governor instead of seeking re-election, according to The Associated Press.
 Lacore defeated Jenny Costa Honeycutt, a Republican who is an ally of President Trump’s, in a district that not only leans conservative but was restructured through gerrymandering to further favor Republicans.
 Democrats had eyed the seat in the First Congressional District, hoping that Lacore’s military background could be an asset. Her ouster as chief of the Navy Reserve during Hegseth’s broader purge of senior military leaders last year gave her a national profile, and Lacore said that her dismissal motivated her to run for office.
 Lacore has spoken in support of codifying Roe v. Wade in federal law, restoring expanded Medicaid benefits and imposing stricter oversight on Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
 Image Credit... Win Mcnamee/Getty Images Nov. 6, 2026, 5:34 p.m. ET Tim Balk 
 Eliott Rodriguez, a South Florida Democrat whose race for the House remains too close to call , filed a lawsuit on Friday in federal court in Miami requesting that the Miami-Dade County elections supervisor, Alina Garcia, recuse herself from any recount process in his race.
 The complaint cited a Miami Herald article that reported Garcia said on election night that Representative María Elvira Salazar, the Republican incumbent, was the winner “with or without a recount.” The complaint also says that Garcia, who is also a Republican, and the congresswoman are friends.
 “We have an election supervisor who is crossing the lines,” Rodriguez said by phone. Garcia’s office and Salazar’s campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
 Nov. 6, 2026, 4:27 p.m. ET Evan Reynolds 
 Election data reporter In the Mississippi Senate race, Scott Colom’s lead over Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, grew to about 2,500 votes on Friday, according to The Associated Press, after three more counties reported votes around 4:10 p.m. Eastern. Colom’s margin has increased by nearly 700 votes today, though just under 1,500 new votes have been reported statewide.

 The next batches of votes from Alaska are expected to be posted on Monday and Tuesday, according to the state’s Division of Elections. These are expected to consist of ballots cast early in-person and by mail.
 The remaining votes, mostly from mail-in ballots, have until Nov. 18 to be counted. At that time, ranked-choice tabulation would begin if the top candidates in the Senate, governor and House races have not received a majority of votes.

 Texas politics reporter Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat who has served in the Texas House for more than 50 years, just announced in the Texas State Capitol that she had enough votes to become speaker next year. Thompson said she would work with Republicans, who are now in the minority party for the first time in more than 20 years, when state lawmakers meet for their next session in January. “I do not have a dictatorship,” she said. 
 Thompson, 87, would be the first Black speaker and first female speaker.
 Image Credit... Lauren McGaughy for The New York Times Nov. 6, 2026, 3:46 p.m. ET Soumya Karlamangla 
 California still has nearly 5 million ballots to count. 
 Image Election workers in Los Angeles County still had more than 700,000 mail ballots to process as of Thursday evening. Credit... Mario Tama/Getty Images In California, more than a third of ballots from Tuesday’s election have yet to be counted, holding up results for the state’s billionaire tax initiative as well as various local races in the state.
 California normally draws attention — and plenty of criticism — for its protracted vote count. But this election, the state’s uncalled races won’t factor into the balance of power in Congress after Democrats won both houses Tuesday in dominant fashion. And far more attention has been paid to Mississippi and Alaska , where Senate races are so tight that Americans are following daily updates.
 In California, there were about 4.8 million ballots left to tally statewide as of Thursday evening, roughly 35 percent of the 13.7 million cast in Tuesday’s election, according to the California secretary of state’s office. Remarkably, some counties, including Sacramento, Riverside and Napa, had more ballots left to count than they had already tallied since Tuesday.
 The reasons for California’s slow count are explained after each election. California relies heavily on mail balloting, which delays the tally because of the labor-intensive work it takes to check signatures, open envelopes and inspect ballots before counting them. The state also accepts mail-in ballots up to seven days after polls close as long as they were postmarked by Election Day.
 California’s leaders take pride in a deliberate process that is meant to make voting easy while keeping elections secure, they say.
 Still, the slow vote count in California has delayed results in pivotal contests once again. It wasn’t until Thursday that The Associated Press called the Los Angeles mayor’s race for Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, over the incumbent, Karen Bass.
 And The A.P. is still waiting for more results before calling the billionaire tax initiative , which would impose a one-time wealth tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in assets. The measure is currently trailing.
 Five of the state’s 52 House races also have yet to be called. Four of them are intraparty battles that will not affect the final House makeup, but the fifth is in the 23rd Congressional District , where Representative Jay Obernolte, a Republican, is locked in an unexpectedly tight contest with Tessa Lynn Hodge, a Democrat.
 California gives counties 30 days from Election Day to count all ballots and certify the results.
 It’s unclear how long it will take for all of the races to be called. Dozens of counties are expected to issue updated results on Friday afternoon.
 Show more Nov. 6, 2026, 3:12 p.m. ET Lauren McGaughy 
 Texas politics reporter In the Texas Capitol today, Senfronia Thompson, who has been in the State House since 1973, will announce she has more than enough support to become speaker. The Texas House press room is packed with lawmakers, staff members and members of the news media awaiting the announcement. 
 Thompson, known affectionately as “Miss T,” would be the first Black speaker in the state. This week’s blue sweep across Texas gave Democrats control of the Texas House for the first time since 2003.

Katie Hobbs’s re-election victory, Democrats will now have a trifecta — both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — for the first time since the mid-1960s. In fact, the Democrats have not had an outright majority in any legislative chamber in Arizona since the early 1990s.

 Reporting from Washington President Trump announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of his mass deportation effort and a perennial target of liberal critics of the Trump administration, would be promoted to be the White House chief of staff, a stunning move to elevate a hard-liner in his staff after a stunning Republican defeat in the midterm election.
 Image Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times Nov. 6, 2026, 1:10 p.m. ET Campbell Robertson 
 Reporting from Mississippi As lawyers descended on Mississippi to watch ballots be counted, Scott Colom, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, spoke to reporters at a senior center in Jackson, Miss. “Listen, they need to accept the results, right?” he said of Republicans. “That’s what our democracy is all about. When people lose, they can’t be sore losers. They have to accept the results.“
 Colom’s lead in the race has grown to more than 2,000 votes, but three days after the election, the race remains too close for The Associated Press to call.
 Image Credit... Rory Doyle for The New York Times Nov. 6, 2026, 12:52 p.m. ET Evan Reynolds 
 Election data reporter The latest vote report from Mississippi was favorable for Scott Colom, the Democratic candidate for Senate, who picked up 74 votes after Wilkinson County reported its tally at around 12:30 p.m. Eastern. He won a batch of votes from Bolivar County by 123 votes. In total, Colom’s statewide margin over the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, now stands at 2,010 votes.

 National political reporter Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Democrat of Michigan, has formed a leadership PAC, which will allow him to raise money to give away to other Democrats. He is naming it Habibi PAC . “Habibi” is an Arabic term of affection — and one that El-Sayed had used to mock Republicans at times on the campaign trail.
 “JD, habibi — there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed said in a victory speech, referring to Vice President JD Vance.
 Image Credit... Todd Heisler/The New York Times Nov. 6, 2026, 12:20 p.m. ET Mack Liederman 
 Breaking news reporter Democrats are now claiming their victories include a majority of all statehouse seats across the country.
 More than 500 seats in state legislatures were flipped blue in Tuesday’s midterms, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, the arm of the party focused on state-level races.
 Democrats have new trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both statehouse chambers — in at least Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. That puts the party in a powerful position to pass state laws.
 Nov. 6, 2026, 12:04 p.m. ET Caroline Soler 
 Election data reporter In three closely watched Arab American communities in Wayne County, Mich., support for Abdul El-Sayed shifted sharply to the left, outperforming past Democratic performance — not just compared with Kamala Harris’s numbers in 2024, but even against the margins received by Joe Biden in 2020.
 These communities were among the places where the uncommitted vote performed particularly well in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary in Michigan, reflecting anger over the Biden administration’s handling of Gaza and Israel.
 In Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, both of which President Trump carried in 2024, El-Sayed’s margins were more than 25 percentage points higher than Biden’s margins from 2020. In Hamtramck, which Harris narrowly won in 2024, El-Sayed’s margin was 85 percentage points — a 13-percentage-point increase from Biden’s margin in 2020.
 Nov. 6, 2026, 11:45 a.m. ET John Yoon 
 Lauren Boebert is locked in an unexpectedly close race in Colorado. 
 Image Representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado at the Capitol in September. She initially gained political fame in 2020 as a gun activist, unseating a more moderate five-term Republican, Scott Tipton. Credit... Kenny Holston/The New York Times Representative Lauren Boebert, a right-wing firebrand who has been in and out of favor with President Trump, was fighting for her seat in an unexpectedly tight race in Colorado. She trailed her Democratic opponent by a few thousand votes as of Friday morning.
 Election analysts had favored Ms. Boebert over her challenger, Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy, in Colorado’s Fourth Congressional District , long considered one of the state’s safest Republican seats.
 That the race has yet to be called three days after the election offered yet another sign of how dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump’s policies has hurt Republicans in the midterms.
 The district encompasses a mix of rural farming and ranching communities on the Great Plains and in the suburban hubs east of Denver.
 Ms. Laubacher, who served on the National Security Council in the Biden administration, was leading in the district’s more populous, suburban counties. She campaigned on ending Mr. Trump’s tariffs, enacting tax cuts for the middle class, strengthening rural hospitals, and fighting corruption.
 Ms. Boebert initially gained political fame in 2020 as a hard-right gun activist, unseating a more moderate five-term Republican, Scott Tipton, in Colorado’s Third District, which is speckled with progressive upscale ski towns but dominated by conservative ranching and working-class communities. She joined the conservative Freedom Caucus that year and later helped lead the Second Amendment Caucus.
 Before being elected to Congress, she had owned a gun-themed restaurant called Shooters Grill in Colorado’s ranch country, where she encouraged her wait staff to carry loaded firearms while serving customers.
 In Washington, she boasted about carrying her Glock handgun and clashed with Democrats from time to time, drawing attention for her fiery statements. Shortly after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, she triggered an alarm while passing through a newly installed metal detector and refusing to allow guards to search her handbag.
 After she won a close re-election in the Third District in 2022, she switched to the state’s more reliably conservative Fourth District for her 2024 campaign and won by about 12 points that year.
 Ms. Boebert had been an ardent Trump supporter, but she fell out of his favor last year over her support for the release of the Epstein files. This year, Mr. Trump had criticized her as “weak,” but then he endorsed her just before the election, calling her a ”MAGA warrior.”

 A Trump-backed candidate keeps a House seat in New York under Republican control. 
 Image Anthony Constantino, an avid supporter of President Trump, will succeed Representative Elise Stefanik in northern New York. Credit... Al Drago for The New York Times Anthony Constantino, a 44-year old sticker mogul who put his loyalty to President Trump at the heart of his campaign, narrowly won a House race to succeed Representative Elise Stefanik, keeping the seat in New York’s North Country under Republican control, according to The Associated Press .
 A first-time candidate who spent roughly $17 million into his self-funded campaign, Mr. Constantino seemed to delight in eschewing political decorum, much like his mentor, Mr. Trump.
 With the race still too close to call on election night, Mr. Constantino nonetheless delivered a 25-minute acceptance speech that was indignant and pugilistic. He told one Republican opponent to “go hide in a hole” and described reporters as “scumbags” and “evil.”
 He closed by pledging to give each of his roughly 1,200 employees a $1,000 bonus, and called upon the leaders of other major companies to do the same.
 It was Mr. Constantino’s penchant for grandiose gestures that gave him visibility in Mr. Trump’s circle. He mounted a 100-foot-wide “VOTE FOR TRUMP” sign atop the headquarters of his company, Sticker Mule, in Amsterdam, N.Y. He later gave the president a life-size bronze statue, and recorded a rap album that he entitled “Thank You President Trump.”
 Democrats and some Republicans saw his political antics and his close ties to the president as a liability, bolstering the hopes of his Democratic opponent, Blake Gendebien, a dairy farmer who hoped to attract enough voters in a district that favored President Trump by 20 points just two years ago.
 Mr. Gendebien, 49, who served as the former vice chairman of the cooperative that produces Cabot cheese, focused on local and economic issues, including expanding rural health care and bringing down the price of diesel for farmers.
 He earned the endorsements of some of the state’s most powerful unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O., Teamsters, teachers’ union and Police Conference of New York. And he was careful to distance himself from Democrats on key issues like energy policy (despite the fact that the party showered him with significant financial and operational support).
 It appeared Mr. Gendebien had some momentum, even slightly surpassing Mr. Constantino in one late-stage poll. But Mr. Constantino prevailed by two percentage points, with The Associated Press calling the race on Friday.
 Mr. Constantino spent much of his campaign attacking his opponent, Mr. Gendebien, sometimes going to unusual lengths. He acknowledged paying private investigators to fly a drone above Mr. Gendebien’s farm to gather what he claimed was evidence that his rival was polluting, showing aerial video footage to reporters. (Mr. Constantino asserted that Mr. Gendebien was under investigation for pollution; state officials said there was no open inquiry.)
 The over-the-top accusation followed a pattern of behavior. Mr. Constantino feuded publicly with those who should have been political allies, from local party officials to the head of the Conservative Party, Gerard Kassar. Mr. Constantino claimed that Mr. Kassar had made a threat to kill him; Mr. Kassar sued for defamation.
 During the primary, Mr. Constantino was so disruptive during a candidates’ forum held by the St. Lawrence County Republican Party that he was removed by the sheriff .
 Mr. Trump nonetheless endorsed Mr. Constantino in the primary, helping him to defeat Robert Smullen, a state assemblyman and former Marine who was the choice of the state Republican Party.
 In the final push, Mr. Trump sent his son and his vice president to Rome, N.Y., for a last-minute rally for Mr. Constantino. In a video message, he called Mr. Constantino “a phenomenal person” and “a winner.”

 Democratic gains could advance an alternative to the Electoral College. 
 Image Voters casting their ballots in Dearborn Heights, Mich., on Tuesday. A state lawmaker said that after Tuesday’s midterm results, “The time is right” to reconsider the Electoral College. Credit... Victor J. Blue for The New York Times Democrats’ midterm victories may raise the chances that enough states sign onto a mechanism that, in theory, could elect the next president effectively by popular vote instead of through the typical rules of the Electoral College.
 The party’s surge in Tuesday’s elections included gaining a hold on the governor’s office and both statehouse chambers in at least five states, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin and Arizona. Those states could join an agreement called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact , which promises that participants would give all their electoral votes to the presidential ticket that wins the national popular vote.
 But the agreement, which has been more popular among Democrats, takes effect only once signed by states representing a majority of the Electoral College, or at least 270 electoral votes, the amount needed to win the presidency. Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have adopted the compact so far, representing 222 electoral votes.
 If four of the states with new Democratic control were to join the agreement, it would tip the group over the 270-vote threshold.
 Lawmakers in key states said on Thursday that they had already begun having conversations this week about introducing legislation to join the agreement in the next session, and were hopeful that they would succeed ahead of 2028. But broadening the compact could present a mighty political lift.
 “The time is right,” Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, said in an interview. “This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation.”
 Still, Democratic lawmakers “can be apprehensive” with a new majority, said Mattie Daughtry, the Democratic president of Maine’s State Senate. She worked on the compact issue for over a decade before her state joined in 2024.
 “The biggest roadblock is convincing them to use these majorities to do big things,” Ms. Daughtry said.
 In 2019, Nevada’s Democratic governor vetoed a bill to join the agreement, saying it could diminish smaller states’ influence in presidential elections.
 Now, it is unclear whether lawmakers will prioritize passing the compact after running campaigns dominated by other concerns, like easing high costs and imposing guardrails on the Trump administration.
 “Time will tell,” said Clinton Anderson, a Democratic state assemblyman in Wisconsin, adding that he planned to reintroduce a compact bill. “I want to make it a priority, but it’s not the thing I heard on the doors I knocked.”
 Kelda Roys, another Democratic lawmaker in Wisconsin, said that her initial attempt to get her state to join the compact in 2009 had been met with hesitancy among people who were unsure exactly what it was. Now, she said, there is a broader public understanding of what problems the Electoral College could present.
 “National popular vote will be something that we’ll prioritize early in the session,” Ms. Roys said.
 The idea for a compact among states to bypass the Electoral College gained traction among legal scholars and supporters after 2000, when George W. Bush won the presidency while losing the national popular vote. Momentum grew in 2016 after a second Republican candidate, Donald J. Trump, won despite losing the popular vote.
 Supporters of the compact said they view the Electoral College as a less democratic mechanism than the popular vote. A YouGov poll conducted in June showed that 56 percent of American adults supported choosing the president via popular vote.
 The compact is also more practical than amending the Constitution and popular among voters, supporters said.
 Opponents and legal experts said the compact would face a slew of court challenges. One obstacle is that compacts traditionally require the approval of Congress and the president, said Derek Muller, an election law expert at Notre Dame Law School who has written about the agreement.
 “It’s a very real possibility that enough states join this compact,” he said. “There will be a lot of challenges.”

 In Mississippi, careful scrutiny of votes in an unexpectedly tight race. 
 Image Voting machines and ballot bags used in the midterm elections remain at the Hinds County Election Commission building in Jackson, Miss. Credit... Rory Doyle for The New York Times Fewer than 2,000 votes separated the candidates for Senate in Mississippi on Thursday, causing a raft of lawyers, campaign operatives and legal observers to descend on county election offices to watch officials count ballots in the contest between Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and her challenger, Scott Colom.
 If he prevails, Mr. Colom, a Democratic district attorney, would be the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. As of Thursday afternoon, he held a lead of 1,813 votes over Ms. Hyde-Smith, a Republican serving her first term.
 In an election when Democrats broke through conservative strongholds to gain majorities in the House and Senate, Mississippi and Alaska are the only remaining states where the Senate races do not yet have a clear victor.
 That there is suspense at all in Mississippi, which has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in more than four decades, has stunned Democrats and Republicans.
 Image Scott Colom, a Democratic district attorney, in Jackson, Miss., on Thursday. Credit... Rory Doyle for The New York Times “I’m glad that the country is starting to see what Mississippi values look like and what Mississippi’s potential is,” said Mr. Colom, as he spoke to reporters in Jackson.
 On social media, Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign said she would remain in the Senate , given that “we believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory.”
 The outcome of the race appears to hinge on what the state has said is an unknown number of affidavit ballots, cast by voters who were either listed as inactive or without proper identification. On Thursday, Michael Watson, the secretary of state, said roughly 3,300 absentee-by-mail ballots were also still outstanding. To count, they must be received within five business days of Nov. 3.
 He did not provide a number for the uncounted affidavit ballots, but said that 6,936 affidavit ballots had been processed. The deadline for counties to certify their election results to the state is Nov. 13.
 Unlike most states, Mississippi law does not allow for a recount of votes in a statewide election.
 In Jackson, the state capital, on Thursday, lawyers, reporters, poll watchers and, at one point Mr. Colom’s wife, milled among the tables in the cramped Hinds County Election Commission headquarters. The commission members had been going through ballots since 7 a.m., working steadily but with little acknowledgment of the intense national scrutiny.
 “I hope they put a pep in their step,” said June Hardwick, a lawyer who supported the Colom campaign.
 Jermal Clark, one of the commissioners, said they had to ensure that they were being thorough and that they were following the law. “To me, everything is going well,” he said. “It’s just congested.”
 Republicans were not taking chances.
 On Thursday, Republican lawyers wrote to election commissioners to demand “the immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Mr. Colom’s legal team responded with their own letter , calling it a request for “unlawful and extraordinary measures” and warning that it risked leading to the unlawful identification of voters.
 Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party and the general counsel of the Republican National Committee, said that lawyers aligned with national Republicans and Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign “will be ready, if necessary, to avail ourselves of every legal option at our disposal, if there is evidence that the law has been violated.”
 Image Republican U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith speaks to guests at her election night watch party on Tuesday in Flowood, Miss. Credit... Sarah Warnock/USA Today Network, via Reuters “We’ve never seen this before in Mississippi — we’ve never seen this volume of affidavit ballots around this state,” Mr. Hurst said. He added, “This race is far from being over.”
 Some Mississippi organizers said it was possible that some of that increase in affidavit ballots might trace back to last July, when the secretary of state’s office announced it would use data from Experian, the credit reporting agency, to help maintain the state’s voter rolls .
 As part of that change, registered voters identified as having a new address were labeled “inactive” until they returned a confirmation card with their new address. Anyone who showed up to vote this year and was marked “inactive” had to fill out an affidavit ballot.
 Cassandra Welchlin, the executive director of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, said her organization was helping to organize rides for students to get to courthouses and ensure their ballot was counted and would be launching ads to remind voters to follow up on their affidavit and mail-in ballots.
 “Is it a little nerve-wracking? Yes,” Ms. Welchlin said. “Because we want to make sure that every vote is counted.”
 Mr. Colom, a district attorney with deep roots in the state, mounted a relentless campaign, energizing the state’s Black voters and coaxing white Democrats and disenchanted conservatives to buy into his message of “Mississippi Matters.”
 Image Election observers watch the vote count at the Hinds County Election Commission in Jackson, Miss. Credit... Rory Doyle for The New York Times Ms. Hyde-Smith saw more than $1 million pour in during the campaign’s last stretch from national groups. President Trump also held a rally in Corinth for Ms. Hyde-Smith and urged Republicans to vote.
 Mr. Colom used Ms. Hyde-Smith’s words against her, making a campaign ad out of her suggestion that voters could choose alternative proteins as meat prices climbed. The tagline “Pick another protein? Pick another senator” became his campaign’s rallying cry in the final days before the election.

 Nithya Raman’s win in Los Angeles adds to the major cities with democratic socialist leaders. 
 Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, Nithya Raman, the new mayor of Los Angeles, Mayor Katie Wilson of Seattle. The New York Times Nithya Raman won the mayoral race in Los Angeles on Thursday, joining the ranks of democratic socialists who have been elected to lead major American cities over the past year.
 Once she takes office, the mayors in the two most-populous American cities and the nation’s capital will be members of the Democratic Socialists of America , a political group of dues-paying members organized around a broad policy platform.
 A strong emphasis on expanding public services, such as housing, health care, child care, public transportation and infrastructure, and heavily taxing corporations and wealthy individuals ties together their positions .
 Here’s what to know:
 Democratic socialists have been elected mayor in several cities. 
 In New York City , Zohran Mamdani’s election last year made him perhaps the most prominent mayor who is a member of the D.S.A. As part of his progressive agenda, he has pushed through a “ rent freeze ” for nearly one million rent-stabilized apartments, fought to tax high-end second homes and expanded a free child care program for 2-year-olds in partnership with Gov. Kathy Hochul.
 In Los Angeles , where the mayor’s race is nonpartisan, Ms. Raman, a city councilwoman, is a member of the D.S.A. An urban planner by training, she promoted an aggressive expansion of the housing supply, advocated zoning changes and called for prioritizing public transit improvements, among other proposals. She will unseat Karen Bass, a more moderate Democrat who has served as mayor since 2022.
 In Seattle , Mayor Katie Wilson, who was elected last year, has described herself as a democratic socialist but is not a D.S.A. member. In office, she has accelerated homeless shelter openings , led the passage of a major transit service expansion and rolled out new investments in preschool programs .
 In Washington, D.C. , Janeese Lewis George, a district councilwoman who is a member of the D.S.A., was elected mayor on Tuesday. She has called for enacting universal child care, building social housing owned by the city, strengthening tenant protections and lowering rental costs for small businesses. She is set to replace Muriel Bowser, a Democrat who is more moderate and did not seek a fourth term.
 In Providence, R.I. , David Morales, a state lawmaker and former professional wrestler who is also a D.S.A. member, was elected mayor on Tuesday. He easily defeated his Republican opponent, David Talan, after running a campaign focused on capping rent hikes, building affordable homes in vacant buildings and on empty lots and demanding that corporations contribute more to funding city services and public schools.
 President Trump responded. 
 After Ms. Raman’s race was called on Thursday, President Trump was asked about the election of democratic socialists. He predicted that people would be unhappy with their policies and said, “It’s going to be a disaster.”
 “Unfortunately, usually that happens so late that you’ll never be able to bring back a city, or a country or a state, when it goes too far,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
